Carpets In Square 2

GeometryAreaConstructions
Game: Two rectangles overlap inside a bigger one; the red pieces always have the same total size as the blue piece, and there is nothing to win or lose.
How to play: Drag A along the bottom edge or F along the right edge, or focus either point and use the arrow keys. Tick “hint” to see the proof lines, tick “names” for the letters, and press Reset to start again.

Drag A or F, or focus one and press the arrow keys (Shift for bigger steps).

Look for the math

Two rectangles lie inside a third one and overlap. No matter how you move their corners, the areas balance in two surprising ways. Here is why.

One centre and one circle

The diagonals of a rectangle — even of a parallelogram — meet at their common midpoint. EFGH and IFJH share the diagonal FH, so their diagonals are equal and their midpoints are the same point O. That point is also the middle of ABCD: it is halfway along FH (the horizontal middle) and halfway along EG (the vertical middle). So E, F, G, I and J all sit the same distance from O, on one circle.

O = (A + C)/2 = (F + H)/2 = (E + G)/2 = (I + J)/2

The applet picks F on BC at 30% of the way from B to C, then draws H opposite F and cuts the circle by the bottom side AB to get E and I. The logic test transcribes those steps from the applet's own bytecode and checks all ten points for nearly two thousand configurations.

Red against blue

With “hint” unticked, the blue quadrilateral HKFL is the part where the two carpets overlap. The six red triangles are the parts of ABCD that neither carpet covers. The page's first claim is

total red area = area of HKFL

Tick “hint” and the picture changes to a different pair: the blue quadrilateral IFGH has half the area of ABCD, and the four red triangles together have the other half. The logic test checked both equalities on a grid of A and F drags and on 500 random boards: they held every time the picture can be drawn.

Adding the two carpets

The page's second claim is about the rectangles themselves:

area(EFGH) + area(IFJH) = area(ABCD)
area(IFGH) = area(EFJH) = area(ABCD)/2

Because the two rectangles share the diagonal FH, each is split by that diagonal into two equal halves; the halves fit together to make exactly the big rectangle. The logic test confirms these formulas across all the same configurations, including when A is dragged so the outer rectangle becomes narrower.

Try moving F to the middle of BC: the inner rectangles become mirror images and the blue shape in hint mode fills exactly half of ABCD. Untick “hint” to watch K and L take over.

Puzzle by Alexander Bogomolny (cut-the-knot.org)
